entries.body:
E90 is the sedan body code for the 2005-2011 BMW 3 Series generation. The same platform also covers the E91 Touring (wagon), E92 (coupe), and E93 (convertible).

Rear-wheel drive unless the car is badged xi, which means xDrive all-wheel drive. Front suspension is a double-pivot MacPherson strut design, rear is a multi-link axle.

The US-market 325i with the N52B25 engine was sold through roughly the 2006-2008 model years, before the LCI (facelift) update changed the front and rear lights, bumpers, and some interior trim.

Source: general public automotive reference knowledge. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, BMW made plenty of running changes within a single model year.

entries.body:
![BMW N52B25 engine under the hood of a 325i Coupé](images/n52b25-engine.jpg)
*Photo by Jussi Korkala, released to the public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:JK_N52B25.jpg).*

2.5L naturally aspirated inline-6, one of the first BMW engines built with a magnesium/aluminum composite block instead of all-aluminum or iron. Uses dual VANOS (variable valve timing) and Valvetronic (variable valve lift, which lets the engine run without a traditional throttle plate for most operating conditions).

Output is roughly 215-218 hp depending on market and model year.

Known wear points across the N52 family, not specific disasters, just things an owner this age should expect eventually:

- Electric water pump and plastic thermostat housing failures
- Plastic coolant pipes and expansion tank cracking with age and heat cycles
- VANOS solenoid issues causing rough idle or a check engine light
- Valve cover gasket seepage, usually shows up as a faint burning smell after the engine's been running a while

Source: general public automotive reference knowledge. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace a failed or failing alternator.
entries.steps:
1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal first, this is a live electrical component.
2. Remove the serpentine belt (see the serpentine belt procedure).
3. Disconnect the electrical connector and the B+ terminal nut from the alternator, note the orientation before you pull anything off.
4. Remove the alternator mounting bolts, these are typically one-time-use torque-to-yield bolts on this engine, buy new ones before you start, don't plan to reuse the old ones.
5. Maneuver the alternator out, it can be a tight fit depending on what else is routed through the engine bay on your specific car.
6. Install the new or rebuilt alternator in reverse order, using new mounting bolts, torque them to spec in the correct stages.
7. Torque the B+ terminal nut to spec, reinstall the belt, reconnect the battery.
8. Start the engine and verify charging voltage is correct before considering the job done.
entries.torque_specs: Alternator mounting bolts: commonly cited as 10 Nm plus an additional 180 degree turn, consistent with a torque-to-yield, one-time-use aluminum bolt design, do not reuse these bolts. B+ terminal nut: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec. Confirm both against your exact year before relying on these numbers.
entries.part_numbers: Alternator, and the mounting bolts if they're the one-time-use type for your car: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Also confirm whether your alternator has an integrated voltage regulator before ordering a replacement, this varies.
entries.tools_needed: Socket set, torque wrench capable of angle-based tightening if your bolts use the torque-to-yield spec, possibly need to loosen other components for clearance depending on your engine bay layout.
entries.notes_warnings: Always disconnect the battery first. Double check the B+ terminal nut is properly torqued, a loose one can arc and melt the connector, which turns a straightforward job into an expensive one. If charging voltage still looks wrong after the swap, check the battery and wiring before assuming the new alternator is also bad, it's an easy trap to fall into.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, cross-checked against public forum discussion of the specific torque spec for this job. Not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the 12V battery. The important part most people miss on this generation of BMW isn't the physical swap, it's registering the new battery afterward.
entries.steps:
1. Note your radio presets and any settings that might reset, some will be retained by the car's memory, some won't.
2. Locate the battery, on this generation it's commonly in the trunk rather than the engine bay, check under the trunk floor panel or side trim.
3. Disconnect the negative terminal first, then the positive, remove any retaining clamp.
4. Remove the old battery, install the new one of the correct type and capacity, reconnect positive first, then negative.
5. **Register the new battery with the car's electrical system.** This generation uses an Intelligent Battery Sensor (IBS) that tracks battery age and condition to manage charging behavior. If you don't register the replacement, the car keeps charging based on the old battery's profile, which noticeably shortens the life of the new one.
6. Registration is typically done either through the car's own iDrive/instrument cluster menu on later software versions, or via diagnostic software (commonly used tools in the community include INPA or similar BMW-specific diagnostic software), confirm what your specific car's software version supports before assuming the in-car menu option exists.
entries.torque_specs: Battery terminal clamps and tray retaining hardware: typically low torque, hand-tight-plus-a-bit is common guidance, verify against RealOEM or dealer spec if you want an exact number.
entries.part_numbers: Battery: confirm the correct capacity (Ah) and type (standard vs AGM) for your car before ordering, this varies by options package, not just by model, verify against RealOEM.com or your door-jamb sticker.
entries.tools_needed: Basic wrench set for the terminals, a battery registration tool or access to the car's menu system, a memory-saver device if you want to avoid losing radio/seat memory settings during the swap.
entries.difficulty: Easy (physical swap) to Medium (if registration requires diagnostic software you don't already have access to)
entries.time_estimate: 20-30 minutes for the physical swap, variable for registration depending on your tools
entries.notes_warnings: This is the step people skip and then wonder why their "new battery" is dead in eight months. If your battery lives in the trunk, also check that the battery vent tube (if equipped) is properly connected, venting matters for AGM batteries in an enclosed space. Disconnecting the battery on this generation can also trigger window/sunroof initialization issues afterward, worth knowing that one-touch window operation sometimes needs to be re-learned per window after a battery disconnect.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, and confirm what registration method your car's software actually supports before starting.

entries.summary: Replace brake pads and, when worn or scored past spec, the rotors, front or rear.
entries.steps:
1. Loosen the wheel bolts slightly before jacking, then jack up the car and support it on stands, remove the wheel.
2. Remove the caliper guide bolts (or the full caliper mounting bracket bolts if you're also replacing the rotor).
3. Lift the caliper off and support it with wire, never let it hang by the brake line, that stresses and can damage the hose.
4. Remove the old pads and anti-rattle clips/shims.
5. If replacing the rotor: remove the caliper bracket, then the rotor, which may be stuck on by corrosion, a few taps with a rubber mallet usually frees it.
6. Clean the hub face before installing a new rotor, debris here causes a wobble that feels like a warped rotor later.
7. Compress the caliper piston back in with a proper tool, on the rear axle some BMWs use an electric parking brake caliper that needs to be wound back with a special tool or retracted electronically, do not just push it like a front piston.
8. Install new pads and clips, reinstall caliper and bracket, torque everything to spec.
9. Pump the brake pedal firmly several times before driving to seat the pads against the rotor.
entries.torque_specs: Caliper guide bolts: around 30 Nm. Caliper bracket-to-knuckle bolts: typically higher, in the 100+ Nm range. Wheel bolts: around 120 Nm. Verify all of these against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact axle and year, front and rear specs differ.
entries.part_numbers: Brake pads, rotors, and anti-rattle clip sets: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, front and rear are different part numbers and some years changed rotor diameter.
entries.tools_needed: Caliper piston compression tool (and the electric parking brake retraction tool/procedure if doing the rear), torque wrench, jack and stands.
entries.notes_warnings: Reset the brake pad wear sensor if your car has one, or the dashboard warning light stays on even with fresh pads. Bed in new pads with a series of gentle stops from moderate speed before relying on hard braking, this transfers an even layer of pad material onto the rotor and meaningfully affects how well they work afterward. If the rear uses an electric parking brake, do not attempt to compress that piston with a standard tool, you can damage the motor.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.procedure_name: Cabin and engine air filter change
entries.summary: Replace the cabin (pollen) filter and the engine intake air filter, two separate, unrelated filters often done together since both are quick.
entries.steps:
### Cabin filter
1. Open the glovebox, remove the side stops/dampers so the glovebox can swing down fully, or remove it entirely depending on your exact trim.
2. Locate the filter housing behind the glovebox, release the retaining clips or cover.
3. Slide the old filter out, noting the airflow direction arrow printed on the frame.
4. Install the new filter in the same orientation, close everything back up.

### Engine air filter
1. Locate the airbox, typically on the side of the engine bay near the front.
2. Release the clips or screws holding the airbox lid closed.
3. Lift the lid, remove the old filter, note its orientation.
4. Wipe out any debris sitting in the bottom of the airbox before installing the new filter.
5. Reinstall the lid and secure the clips/screws.
entries.torque_specs: No meaningful torque specs, these are clip and screw fasteners, hand-tight is correct for essentially all of them.
entries.part_numbers: Cabin filter and engine air filter: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, cabin filters especially have variants (with or without activated charcoal) depending on trim.
entries.tools_needed: None beyond basic hand tools, this is one of the easier jobs on the car.
entries.notes_warnings: Pay attention to the airflow direction arrow on the cabin filter, installing it backward reduces airflow and defeats some of the filtration. If the cabin filter housing has standing water or visible mold when you open it, check the cowl drain area for a clog, a blocked drain is a common cause and just replacing the filter won't fix the underlying issue.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Drain and replace the engine coolant as routine service, or because the system was opened for other work.
entries.steps:
1. Let the engine cool completely before opening any part of the cooling system, this is genuinely dangerous hot.
2. Remove the engine undertray if present.
3. Open the radiator drain petcock, or disconnect the lower radiator hose, into a drain pan. Loosen the expansion tank cap to help it drain faster.
4. Close the drain petcock or reconnect the hose once fully drained.
5. Refill with BMW-spec coolant mixed to the correct ratio, never use a generic universal coolant, the wrong chemistry attacks the plastic components in this cooling system.
6. Bleed the system: this engine needs air purged properly through the bleed screw on the expansion tank or thermostat housing, or it will run hot and you'll think you have a different problem.
7. Run the engine to operating temperature with the heater on full blast, this helps push trapped air out. Check for leaks, then top off the level once the car has fully cooled.
entries.torque_specs: Hose clamps and any fasteners disturbed during the drain: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec, these vary by exactly what you're touching.
entries.part_numbers: BMW-spec blue antifreeze, correct ratio for this generation: verify exact OEM part number against RealOEM.com using your VIN.
entries.tools_needed: Drain pan, BMW-spec coolant, a cooling system bleed/fill tool makes for a much cleaner bleed if you have access to one.
entries.notes_warnings: If you're already in here and the thermostat housing or water pump looks original, strongly consider replacing them proactively rather than coming back into the same job in a year. Both are known weak points on this engine family. Never skip the bleed step, trapped air is the most common reason a coolant change "doesn't fix" an overheating issue.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the plastic coolant expansion tank, a known weak point on this engine family, it cracks over time from repeated heat and pressure cycling, usually showing up as a slow coolant loss with no visible puddle.
entries.steps:
1. Let the engine cool completely before opening any part of the cooling system.
2. Relieve system pressure by slowly loosening the expansion tank cap.
3. Drain coolant down below the level of the tank, you don't need to fully drain the whole system for this job, just enough that coolant isn't pouring out when the tank is disconnected.
4. Disconnect the hoses from the tank, note which hose goes where, they're not always obviously different.
5. Disconnect the low coolant level sensor connector if your tank has one built in.
6. Remove the tank's mounting bolts or clips, lift it out.
7. Transfer the level sensor to the new tank if it's a separate part, or confirm the new tank includes one if that's how your car is equipped.
8. Install the new tank, reconnect hoses and the sensor, refill coolant to spec.
9. Bleed the system per the standard coolant bleed procedure, trapped air here causes the same overheating symptoms as a full coolant change done without bleeding.
entries.torque_specs: Mounting bolts and hose clamps: low torque, hand-tight-plus-a-quarter-turn is common guidance for the clamps, verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for the mounting hardware.
entries.part_numbers: Coolant expansion tank, and the low coolant level sensor if it's a separate part on your car: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Some aftermarket tanks are known to have the same cracking issue as the original design, worth checking owner discussion on whether a specific aftermarket brand has a better track record before you buy the cheapest option.
entries.tools_needed: Drain pan, basic hand tools, BMW-spec coolant to refill.
entries.notes_warnings: Inspect the hoses connecting to the tank while you're in there, if they're original and brittle, replacing them at the same time saves a second coolant drain and bleed later. Never use non-BMW-spec coolant, the wrong chemistry attacks the plastic components throughout this cooling system, which is part of why these plastic parts fail as often as they do.

entries.summary: Replace engine oil and the oil filter element as part of routine service.
entries.steps:
1. Warm the engine for a few minutes so the oil flows freely, then shut it off.
2. Remove the engine undertray.
3. Remove the drain plug and let the oil fully drain into a pan, this takes longer than people expect, don't rush it.
4. Remove the oil filter housing cap (large plastic cap near the front of the engine), replace the filter element and both O-rings on the cap.
5. Reinstall the drain plug with a new crush washer, and the filter cap.
6. Refill with the correct oil spec and quantity, start the engine, check for leaks around the drain plug and filter cap, then check the level once settled.
entries.torque_specs: Oil drain plug: around 25 Nm. Oil filter housing cap: around 25 Nm. Verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact year, these are commonly cited figures, not pulled from your specific car's documentation.
entries.part_numbers: Oil filter element and drain plug crush washer: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN. Oil spec: BMW Longlife-01 5W-30 is the commonly cited spec for this engine generation, capacity is roughly 6.5 liters with filter, confirm both against your owner's manual.
entries.tools_needed: Oil filter housing wrench (typically 36mm), drain pan, torque wrench.
entries.notes_warnings: Don't overtighten the filter housing cap, it's plastic and cracks easily, especially once it's a few years old. Let the oil drain fully before refilling, a partial drain leaves old oil and contaminants behind.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace the oil filter housing itself, not just the filter element inside it. This is a different, bigger job than a routine oil change, done when the housing has cracked or is leaking from somewhere other than the cap O-rings.
entries.steps:
1. Drain the oil first, same as for a routine oil change, there's no way to remove the housing with oil still in the system.
2. Remove whatever is in the way for access, on this engine that commonly includes intake ducting and sometimes the alternator or its bracket, depending on exactly how the housing is oriented on your specific engine bay layout.
3. Disconnect the oil pressure/level sensor connectors if they're mounted on the housing.
4. Remove the housing mounting bolts, noting their positions, they're not all identical length on some versions.
5. Lift the housing away from the block, have a drain pan ready, there's always residual oil that comes with it.
6. Clean the mating surface on the block thoroughly.
7. Install the new housing with a new gasket/seal, torque the mounting bolts evenly in a crisscross pattern.
8. Reconnect sensors and reinstall anything removed for access, refill with oil and a new filter element, check for leaks once running.
entries.torque_specs: Housing mounting bolts: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact engine revision, this varies by whether your housing uses a separate gasket or an integrated seal design.
entries.part_numbers: Oil filter housing assembly and mounting gasket/seal: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, there have been revised versions of this housing across the production run addressing earlier cracking issues, worth checking if a superseded part number applies to your car.
entries.tools_needed: Standard socket set, drain pan, possibly extensions/universal joints depending on access clearance.
entries.time_estimate: 2-3 hours depending on what needs to come off for access
entries.notes_warnings: If you're replacing the housing because the old one cracked, inspect it once it's out, cracking at the same spot repeatedly across many owners' cars is a known pattern on this engine family and is worth researching before you reinstall the exact same design if a revised part number exists. Don't skip cleaning the mating surface, a rushed cleanup here is the most common reason for a comeback leak.

entries.summary: Replace the accessory belt that drives the alternator, water pump, power steering pump, and AC compressor off the front of the engine.
entries.steps:
1. Note the belt routing before removing anything, either photograph it or check the routing diagram sticker under the hood, you'll need it to install the new one correctly.
2. Use a breaker bar or a dedicated tensioner tool on the tensioner pulley to release belt tension.
3. Slip the belt off the pulleys, starting with whichever is easiest to reach.
4. While it's off, spin the tensioner and idler pulleys by hand, feel for roughness or play, replace them if anything feels off, they're cheap compared to a belt failure later.
5. Route the new belt exactly per the diagram, the last pulley you route it onto is usually the alternator or AC compressor.
6. Release the tensioner slowly and confirm the belt has seated properly in every pulley groove before starting the engine.
entries.torque_specs: Tensioner pulley mounting bolt: verify against RealOEM or dealer spec for your exact engine revision before relying on a memorized number, this is not a high-stakes fastener in terms of failure mode but it's still worth getting right.
entries.part_numbers: Serpentine belt and tensioner/idler pulleys: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, there are revisions across the production run of this engine.
entries.tools_needed: Tensioner release tool or a long breaker bar, flashlight to see the routing clearly.
entries.notes_warnings: A mis-routed belt can spin the AC compressor or alternator backward, which is not something you want to discover after you've already started the engine. Double check the routing diagram before you pull the old belt off, not after.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year.

entries.summary: Replace a leaking valve cover gasket, a common age-related leak on this engine, usually shows up as a faint burning smell or visible seepage down the back of the engine.
entries.steps:
1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal.
2. Remove the engine cover and intake components in the way, on this engine that typically includes some combination of the ignition coil connectors, coil packs themselves, and nearby wiring harness clips.
3. Disconnect the VANOS solenoid connectors near the front of the cover if they're in the way of cover removal.
4. Remove the valve cover bolts in the reverse of the tightening sequence below, lift the cover off carefully, the gasket is often integrated into the cover itself on this engine rather than a separate piece.
5. Clean the cylinder head mating surface thoroughly, any old gasket material or oil residue left behind causes a new leak almost immediately.
6. Install the new cover/gasket, hand-thread all bolts first before torquing any of them.
7. Torque bolts in a crisscross pattern working from the center bolts outward, in stages rather than going straight to full torque on each bolt.
8. Reconnect everything in reverse, reconnect the battery, start the engine and check for leaks after it's warmed up.
entries.torque_specs: This engine was built with two different valve cover designs across its production run, a plastic cover and a magnesium/aluminum cover, and they have different specs. Plastic cover bolts: commonly cited around 9 Nm. Magnesium cover bolts: commonly cited around 7 Nm plus an additional 90 degree turn, and those bolts are typically a one-time-use, torque-to-yield design, don't reuse them. Confirm which cover type you actually have before using either number, and verify against RealOEM or dealer spec regardless.
entries.part_numbers: Valve cover (with integrated gasket, if your design uses one) and cover bolts if they're the one-time-use type: verify exact OEM part numbers against RealOEM.com using your VIN, this is one of the areas where getting the wrong variant for your specific cover type is an easy mistake.
entries.tools_needed: Torque wrench capable of low Nm values and angle-based tightening if your cover uses the torque-to-yield bolts, basic hand tools for the intake/coil components in the way.
entries.time_estimate: 1.5-2.5 hours depending on what's in the way on your specific car
entries.notes_warnings: Identify your cover type (plastic vs magnesium/aluminum) before you start, the wrong torque spec on the wrong bolt type either leaves it loose enough to leak immediately or over-torques a one-time-use bolt. Never reuse torque-to-yield bolts if that's what your cover uses. Take photos of connector routing before you start disconnecting things, there are more clips and connectors in this area than you'll remember afterward.
entries.source: General public automotive reference knowledge, cross-checked against public forum and retailer-guide discussion of this specific job (BMW enthusiast forums, Pelican Parts' public E90 tech article index). Not extracted from any manual. Verify specifics for your exact build and year, and confirm your actual cover type before relying on either torque figure.
